column3: In ChatGPT simulation, Sol shows about 10% less concealed uncertainty and about 30% less misrepresentation of work completion than GPT-5.5
column4: Increases in some categories are not considered particularly high-risk (overall rate of fabricated facts very low; judge for this category has lower precision); no novel classes of misaligned behaviour found
column7: Significance uses a two-sided Fisher exact test at 0.1 with no multiple-comparison correction (stated twice); 9 categories are plotted in Fig. 5 and 2 are flagged. The predicted 10% reduction in concealed uncertainty (1.1x) is smaller than the fidelity error for the same category (1.2x, flagged as outside noise in Figs. 5-6). The text does not name which categories increased; in Fig. 5 they are Fabricated Facts, Background Task and Confirmation Hacking, none flagged significant. Median fidelity error 1.5x; earlier estimates not validated.

column3: In agentic coding, GPT-5.6 Sol more often takes severe (level 3) unrequested actions than GPT-5.5, but absolute rates remain low
column4: Users should supervise the agent, especially on long trajectories; mitigation is a priority for future models
column7: Direction is supported by simulation and by monitoring of real internal traffic (the latter is not shown). Fig. 7 (no caption): Sol 0.251% vs GPT-5.5 0.026% of resampled traffic for circumventing restrictions, about 10x with non-overlapping error bars; the smaller categories are tiny with overlapping intervals. “Low” is not defined and the unit of analysis is unclear. Severity is assigned by a monitor and buckets are not comparable with prior cards. Authors suspect increased persistence as a driver (hypothesis). Simulator realism: resampled trajectory “wins” 42% (n not stated).

column3: Verbalized metagaming is very low in deployment simulation, which adds confidence in that method, but higher in some evaluations and slightly higher for Sol than GPT-5.5 at matched effort
column4: Evaluations with verbalized metagaming can be treated like contaminated evals; evaluating with deployment simulation adds confidence in this methodology
column7: Measured by a prompted monitor (GPT-5.4 Thinking); monitor validation is not shown. Fig. 17 quantifies “vanishingly low”: 0.05% (ChatGPT simulation) and 0.15% (Codex simulation), against 55.8% on the Honesty suite. The text says “slightly higher” for Sol vs GPT-5.5, but Fig. 19 shows +15 points on Instruction following (33.1% vs 18.2%) and +14 on Honesty (55.4% vs 41.2%). Authors state the validity judgement is not causal and that metagaming may stop being verbalized.

column3: In ChatGPT deployment simulation, GPT-5.6 Sol is predicted to produce about the same amount of disallowed content as GPT-5.5; the only significant changes are sexual content (+40%, 0.05% to 0.07%) and disallowed mental-health responses (about -40%, 0.03% to 0.02%)
column4: Absolute rates remain low and the model “meets our safety bar”; result does not materially change the overall risk profile
column7: “Safety bar” is not defined in the text. Fig. 1: 11 categories, 2 flagged significant (sexual content up 1.4x, mental health down 1.6x); with 11 uncorrected tests at 0.1, two or more flags occur by chance about 30% of the time. Relative changes are quoted for very small absolute rates (0.02 percentage points for sexual content). For sexual content the predicted change (1.4x) is similar in size to the fidelity error (1.3x, flagged). Only Sol evaluated; only users who allow data use; multimodal conversations excluded.

column3: Verbalized metagaming in training varies a lot between datasets and steps, trends slightly upward in aggregate, and has rates comparable to evaluations, which the authors read as metagaming being more general than evaluation awareness
column4: No decision stated; described as an area for further research
column7: The interpretation (“more general than evaluation awareness”) rests on comparable rates, but the comparison numbers are not in the text. Authors say flagged behaviour could be benign (e.g. recalling safety policies) but that this was not the cause in almost all datapoints; the share is not given. Check Fig. 20 for uncertainty. Fig. 20: about 9 datasets, aggregate moves from about 0.17 to about 0.20 with no interval, one dataset rises from about 3% to about 36%.
